display.title: Episode 408: The Storyteller, Chapter 2 (Erev Chanukah 5750)
display.summary_short: Uncle Yossi's pre-Chanukah show: what the Chanukah candles whisper to children, Shema with a Beis Yaakov class, and chapter 2 of the Baal Shem Tov's storyteller.
display.summary_long: Recorded the week Chanukah 5750 began. Uncle Yossi opens with the Rebbe's teaching that the Chanukah lights 'whisper' a message: just as each candle lights up the room, every child must bring the light of Torah and mitzvos into a dark world, and add more light every day (maalin bakodesh). After the Hakochainik march, a third-grade class from Beis Yaakov of Boro Park recites the Shema, and everyone drops coins in the pushka. Story time continues 'The Storyteller': Rabbi Yehuda, the Baal Shem Tov's personal shamash, was told on the Baal Shem Tov's last day to travel and tell stories, and that this would make him rich. His first customer, an innkeeper, pays three kopecks; Rabbi Yehuda refuses to give up. The show closes with a listener's letter, the timing of Chanukah and Shabbos candles on Friday, and a reminder to invite friends who have no menorah.
display.lesson: Be like a Chanukah candle: bring the light of Torah and mitzvos to others, and add a little more light every day.

display.title: Water, Hashem's Precious Gift: Why We Wash Negel Vasser
display.summary_short: Why water is one of Hashem's greatest gifts, and how its special power of purity is why we wash negel vasser every morning.
display.summary_long: A short talk from the Tzivos Hashem radio show. Uncle Yossi explains that life on earth depends on water, and that Hashem placed the sun exactly far enough away that the oceans neither boil nor freeze. We pray for rain and say a brachah before drinking. Water also has a spiritual power to make us pure: the Kohanim washed their hands and feet from the copper basin at the entrance of the Mishkan, and we begin each day by washing negel vasser so we can serve Hashem in purity. The clip ends by introducing a story about Rabbi Akiva and this mitzvah, which is not included.
display.lesson: Appreciate Hashem's gift of water, and start every day by washing negel vasser so you serve Hashem in purity.

display.title: The Baal Shem Tov to the Rescue
display.summary_short: Years after the Baal Shem Tov's passing, a boy born through his blessing is kidnapped, and a mysterious 'bishop' brings him home.
display.summary_long: A childless Chassid receives the Baal Shem Tov's blessing for a son, on condition that the boy is always watched. Three years after the Baal Shem Tov passes away, the babysitter steps out for a moment to see a dancing bear, and five-year-old Moshele disappears. The father turns to Adel, the Baal Shem Tov's daughter, who asks her father at his resting place and returns with instructions: ask at every inn. At last an innkeeper reveals that a local poritz has taken the boy to raise him as a non-Jew, and is waiting for the bishop to arrive. The father stops a bishop's carriage on the road; the 'bishop' convinces the poritz that a Jewish child will always run to a fellow Jew, and the boy runs straight into his father's arms. Then the real bishop arrives late. Adel tells the father that he gave her father a hard job and must be more careful.
display.lesson: A Rebbe continues to care for his Chassidim after his passing, and a Jewish child always stays connected to his people. A tzaddik's instructions must be followed carefully.

advisories.note: A five-year-old is kidnapped; resolved happily.
The poritz plans to convert the boy.

display.title: The Drunken Father
display.summary_short: Naftali tries to cure his father's drinking by showing him a drunk in the street, but the father only asks where to get such a good drink. A story with no happy ending and an important lesson.
display.summary_long: Broadcast on 4 Iyar 5742, the week of Parshas Acharei-Kedoshim. Uncle Yossi explains the Alter Rebbe's teaching to 'live with the times': learn each day's portion of the weekly parsha and take a lesson from it. The parsha warns not to follow the ways of Egypt and Canaan; Hashem showed us how they lived only so that we would see it is not our way. Then comes a story that 'has no happy ending'. Naftali, a fine, respectful boy, is ashamed that his father drinks too much. He leads his father to a drunk lying in the street, hoping he will see how awful it is, but the father bends down and asks the drunk where he got such a good drink. Uncle Yossi ties it back: the Torah shows us bad ways only so we can reject them, and we should be a living example of how pleasant a life of Torah and mitzvos is.
display.lesson: Seeing how others live should teach us what not to copy; we are meant to be an example, not to imitate.

display.title: The Melave Malka Special Guest
display.summary_short: How the Alter Rebbe's script began on Rosh Chodesh Shevat, and how a hidden tzaddik's Melave Malka guest turned out to be Eliyahu HaNavi.
display.summary_long: For the week of Rosh Chodesh Shevat, the storyteller explains its anniversary: the Maggid of Mezritch asked the Alter Rebbe to design letters for sifrei Torah, tefillin and mezuzos that satisfy every opinion, and the new script was first used on Rosh Chodesh Shevat; Rabbi Zusha of Anipoli, told of it from Heaven, had his scribe Reb Moshe Sofer write it too. The story then follows that scribe when he was still a hidden tzaddik, working as the supervisor in Reb Yankel's distillery. Every Motzaei Shabbos the two shared Melave Malka. Along the way the storyteller explains why Melave Malka matters: the Gemara's teaching, a warm dish, Miriam's well, Dovid HaMelech's thanksgiving meal and the luz bone. One week Reb Yankel is too busy, goes to find Moshe late at night, and sees a radiant old man at his table. Moshe admits it was Eliyahu HaNavi, who told him to reveal himself and become a teacher, and children announce the new Rebbe when he arrives.
display.lesson: Make Melave Malka every week, even a small bite, and go out of your way to help someone who needs it.

display.title: Tanya Shiur 29: Shivisi Hashem L'negdi Tamid and Tanya Chapter 13 (Elul)
display.summary_short: A Yiddish shiur: the Alter Rebbe's Shulchan Aruch on waking up before the King, Tanya chapter 13 on the beinoni, and an Elul talk on crowning Hashem on Rosh Hashanah.
display.summary_long: Shiur 29 in Rabbi Yosef Goldstein's Yiddish Tanya series, recorded in Elul. Part 1 studies Shulchan Aruch HaRav, Hilchos Hashkamas HaBoker 1:4-5. On waking, one should think before Whom one lies: the King of kings stands over him, so he rises with alacrity, and 'Shivisi Hashem l'negdi tamid' is a great principle of the Torah. Stories illustrate it: the young Tzemach Tzedek in the Alter Rebbe's home, the Baal Shem Tov's father's words 'fear nothing but G-d', and Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakai's deathbed blessing that his students fear Heaven as much as they fear people. Part 2 continues Tanya chapter 13: the beinoni, in whom the yetzer tov and yetzer hara are both 'judges', and Hashem's help that lets the G-dly soul prevail. Part 3 is an Elul talk: Rosh Hashanah as accepting Hashem as King (malchiyos), and the Chassidic custom of taking stock of the year from Chai Elul.
display.lesson: Remember constantly that Hashem stands before you; that awareness brings alacrity, fear of Heaven and joy in serving Him.

display.title: Three Din Torahs: The Hidden Tzaddik of Berditchev
display.summary_short: A Yiddish story. Why did Rabbi Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev honor the funeral of a man the whole town thought was a miser? He tells of three cases that came before him.
display.summary_long: Told in Yiddish. When Reb Dovid, a rich man everyone in Berditchev considered stingy, passes away, the Chevra Kadisha wants to charge his family extra, but Rabbi Levi Yitzchak forbids it and himself attends the funeral, and the whole town follows. Afterwards he explains with three din Torahs. First, Reb Dovid secretly replaced the five thousand rubles a wine merchant had lost, saving the man's life, and refused to take the money back when the real finder repented. Second, he paid the wife of a poor man who had pretended to have a job with Reb Dovid, and refused repayment. Third, he cancelled a loan because, he said, Hashem as guarantor had already repaid him. Reb Dovid gave in secret, so people thought he was a miser; in truth he was a tzaddik.
display.lesson: Do not judge people by how they appear; the greatest tzedakah is often given in secret.

display.title: Red Ivan, Part 1
display.summary_short: Beryl the merchant loves his money and asks a tzaddik for a blessing for a long journey. He is told to daven three times a day and to send regards to a red-bearded man named Ivan.
display.summary_long: The storyteller opens with a lesson from Bereishis: Hashem creates the world anew every second, like a stretched rubber band that would snap back if released, so Hashem is always with us and we can trust Him. In every generation He also gives us tzaddikim who see further than we do. Beryl, a merchant who keeps mitzvos but hates giving tzedakah, asks the holy Reb Shmuel for a blessing before a long trip. Reb Shmuel tells him to daven three times a day and, oddly, to send regards to a red-haired, red-bearded man called Ivan if he meets him. On the way home Beryl pays to stop the wagon so he can daven Mincha in a forest, and is left behind. He reaches an inn and learns that robbers attacked the wagon he had been on. When the robbers' red-bearded leader, Ivan, walks in, Beryl must decide whether to follow the tzaddik's strange instruction. To be continued.
display.lesson: Trust in Hashem, daven even when it is hard, and follow a tzaddik's instructions.

advisories.note: Robbers boast of robbing and killing the wagon passengers (reported, not described).
The other passengers are killed off-scene.
